clue.text: Blow up? It can with dad back in a position of authority!

indicators.note: in says one piece sits inside the other
something blown up is shattered to pieces, so these words are reassembled
back says the word for father is turned round

parts.note: dad is pa

explanation.surface: A child urges blowing something up while Dad is away, all in a bid for authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow up?' rearranges IT CAN; 'back' turns PA into AP, which goes 'in' that mix. The rank stands for the person who holds it; the puzzle's theme is fictional captains.
explanation.definitionFit: A captain holds command of a ship, team or army company, a recognised rank of command.

clue.text: Superpower liberating Crimea peninsula finally

indicators.note: liberating frees the letters of the place name to form a new order
finally picks the closing letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A superpower frees the Crimean peninsula at last.
explanation.definitionFit: The USA is the world's leading superpower, commonly called by the continent's name.

clue.text: Turkey dung tipped over host

parts.note: TR is the international vehicle code for Turkey

indicators.note: tipped over in a down clue means the word is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: dung is poo

explanation.surface: A turkey's droppings get knocked over onto the host of a dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'host' is not the party-giver but a multitude, as in a host of angels or soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A host is an army or large band, and a troop is a body of soldiers.

clue.text: Covers batting square, upsetting game Essex openers

parts.note: a batter in cricket is in
S is a short form for square in measurements

indicators.note: upsetting in a down clue turns the game's letters upside down

parts.note: RU is rugby union

indicators.note: openers takes the first two letters of the county

explanation.surface: A cricket report: batting on the square, while a rival game upsets Essex's opening batsmen.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket scene is a decoy: the square is the central pitch area, and Essex is an English county side. Here 'openers' takes two letters, ES.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurer covers a person against loss, so to protect with a policy is to cover.

clue.text: A quick kiss, embracing a firm, gorgeous bird

indicators.note: embracing says the kiss wraps round the other letters

parts.note: a quick kiss is a peck
CO is company, a firm

explanation.surface: A peck on the cheek while hugging a business, then praise for a lovely bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The male peafowl, famous for its spectacular tail, is the archetypal gorgeous bird.

clue.text: Rambling diatribe from Her Majesty

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen
a diatribe is a rant

explanation.surface: The Queen delivers a long, rambling tirade.
explanation.walkthrough: The order is reversed: the diatribe comes 'from' the Queen, so ER is written first.
explanation.definitionFit: Errant means wandering or roaming, as a knight errant travels in search of adventure.

clue.text: Solution for one who cannot bear clubs?

definitions.text: Solution for one who cannot bear clubs?

parts.words: Solution for one who cannot bear clubs?
parts.note: a golfer who cannot stand carrying clubs could use a motorised cart instead; 'bear' is carry, not tolerate

explanation.walkthrough: 'cannot bear' suggests dislike; it means physically unable to carry the golf bag.
explanation.definitionFit: A small motorised cart that carries a golfer's bag round the course in place of a human bag-carrier.

clue.text: Floral wreath Penny laid in Swiss Cottage

indicators.note: laid in says the coin is placed inside the house

parts.note: a chalet is a Swiss cottage

explanation.surface: Someone named Penny lays a flower wreath in a London place called Swiss Cottage.
explanation.walkthrough: Swiss Cottage is also a district of north London, which disguises the plain meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplet is a garland or circlet of flowers worn on the head.

clue.text: Britons go nuts when drunk, start chanting

indicators.note: drunk suggests the words stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: Drunken British fans go wild and begin chanting.
explanation.definitionFit: To break into song is idiomatically to begin singing suddenly, so it matches starting a chant.

clue.text: In terms of regular features, he plumbed the depths

indicators.note: regular features takes every other letter of the phrase before it

explanation.surface: Speaking regularly, someone sank to deep lows.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Nemo commands the submarine Nautilus in Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Verne's submarine captain literally explored the ocean depths, a play on the idiom for sinking low.

clue.text: Teddy's big idea: turn informer about a Communist

indicators.note: about says the informing word goes round the others

parts.note: to squeal is to inform on someone
a red is a Communist

explanation.surface: A grand plan: inform on a Communist.
explanation.walkthrough: Teddy is US President Theodore Roosevelt, not a toy bear.
explanation.definitionFit: Theodore Roosevelt's domestic programme was called the Square Deal, his signature policy.

clue.text: One smoked plenty of them here untipped

indicators.note: untipped removes the tip at each end of the word

parts.note: the grid holds many captains, and another name for captains is skippers

explanation.surface: A smoker recalls many cigarettes here without filter tips.
explanation.walkthrough: 'them' points to the theme: the grid is full of captains. 'untipped' sounds like filterless cigarettes, but strips the first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A kipper is a herring that has been split, salted and smoked.

clue.text: Reasonable review of Ibsen's leading characters in Little Eyolf

indicators.note: a review looks over the letters again in a new order
leading characters takes the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: A theatre critic gives a fair review of the main roles in an Ibsen play.
explanation.walkthrough: Little Eyolf is a play by Henrik Ibsen; 'review' rearranges IBSENS to SENSIB.
explanation.definitionFit: Sensible and reasonable are synonyms: both describe sound, practical judgement.

clue.text: Out of favour, Spanish king's daughter given endless criticism — incredible!

indicators.note: in favour is in, so out of favour drops those two letters

parts.note: an infanta is a daughter of a Spanish king

indicators.note: endless drops the final letter

parts.note: stick is criticism, as in taking stick

explanation.surface: A Spanish princess falls from grace and is hounded by critics; amazing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of favour' looks like the princess's disgrace, but removes IN. Stick is British slang for harsh criticism.
explanation.definitionFit: Fantastic and incredible both describe something extraordinary, hard to believe.

clue.text: Essentially, Terry-Thomas's cad left imprisoned; what a choker!

indicators.note: essentially takes the central letters of the name
imprisoned says the letter is held inside the cad

parts.note: a rotter is a cad
L is left

explanation.surface: Terry-Thomas's caddish character is jailed; what a disappointment.
explanation.walkthrough: Terry-Thomas was a British actor who played cads and said 'rotter'. The middle two of TERRYTHOMASS are TH.
explanation.definitionFit: A strangler chokes his victim, so the person doing the choking fits the exclamation.

clue.text: Explorer very dry, having packed cape

indicators.note: having packed says the cape is stowed inside

parts.note: so means very
C is cape on maps
TT, teetotal, means dry

explanation.surface: An explorer, abstemious, packs a cape for the trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Falcon Scott, Antarctic explorer, was also Captain Scott, fitting the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Robert Scott led the doomed polar expedition, making him a famous explorer.

clue.text: You and I would welcome the Inland Revenue; that's unusual!

indicators.note: welcome says the tax office is taken inside

parts.note: we'd is you and I would
IR is the Inland Revenue, the former UK tax authority

explanation.surface: Someone says we'd welcome the tax inspector, which would be strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Weird and unusual are synonyms describing something strange or out of the ordinary.

clue.text: What holds up laciest pants?

indicators.note: pants as British slang means rubbish, so the letters are poor and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: What keeps up the laciest underwear?
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like underwear (in Britain, knickers) but signals an anagram as slang for useless.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretchy elastic in a waistband keeps underwear from falling down.

clue.text: Special time to clamp down on breaking news?

parts.note: T is time
to oppress is to clamp down on

explanation.surface: A special moment for authorities to suppress a news story.
explanation.walkthrough: Stop press is the late news slot added to a paper after printing began.
explanation.definitionFit: The stop-press column carried news that broke too late for the main pages.

clue.text: It delivers coffee to drink; looks fresh!

parts.note: a perk is a percolator, which brews coffee
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: A cup of coffee to drink and someone looks livelier.
explanation.definitionFit: To perk up is to become more lively or brighter, looking refreshed.

clue.text: Held up in Languedoc? Cor! I say! It's hot!

indicators.note: Held up says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A traveller held up in southern France exclaims about the heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held up' in a down clue reads the letters upwards; it looks like a delay.
explanation.definitionFit: The sirocco is a hot dusty wind blowing from North Africa across the Mediterranean.

clue.text: A name for Le Pen that is an indication of falling moral standards

parts.note: nom is French for name, the word the French politician would use
IE, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A name linked to French nationalist Le Pen signals declining morals.
explanation.walkthrough: Marine Le Pen is a French politician, so her word for name is the French nom.
explanation.definitionFit: Anomie is a sociological term for the breakdown of social and ethical norms.

clue.text: Crones blocking way in battleground

indicators.note: blocking says the crones stand round the other letters

parts.note: hags are crones
ST is street, a way

explanation.surface: Old women obstruct the road in a field of battle.
explanation.walkthrough: Hastings, on England's south coast, gives its name to the battle of 1066.
explanation.definitionFit: The Battle of Hastings in 1066 saw the Norman conquest of England.

clue.text: Observation on gospel

parts.note: re means on or concerning
Mark is one of the four gospels

explanation.surface: A comment on scripture.
explanation.definitionFit: A remark is a comment, something observed aloud, so observation fits.

clue.text: One PM at one time is one one above one

definitions.meaning: John ... was British Prime Minister in the 1990s
one rank above 1-across: the army officer ranked just above a captain

explanation.walkthrough: The last 'one' is 1-across, the captain; a major ranks one above.
explanation.definitionFit: John Major was PM, and a major is the military rank directly above captain.

clue.text: Scent smelt unusually suggestive of citrus fruit?

indicators.note: unusually says the letters come out in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A perfume with an odd smell hints at citrus.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme goes 'Oranges and lemons, say the bells of St Clement's', a London church.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme links the church with oranges and lemons, so the name evokes citrus.

clue.text: Raise the standard, boy!

definitions.meaning: to lift with a lifting device, as a car
the Union flag, Britain's national flag

explanation.walkthrough: Captain Jack Sparrow and Captain Jack Harkness also fit the captains theme.
explanation.definitionFit: To jack up is to lift; the Union Jack is the flag; Jack is a boy's name.

clue.text: Will break up cartels

indicators.note: break up says the cartels are split and their letters regrouped

explanation.surface: A determined effort to dismantle business cartels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' looks like determination or a verb; it is Will Scarlet of Robin Hood's band.
explanation.definitionFit: Will Scarlet was one of Robin Hood's Merry Men, so the surname completes the name.

clue.text: Bird-box argy-bargy

parts.note: to spar is to box
argy-bargy is British slang for a noisy quarrel, a row

explanation.surface: A noisy quarrel over a bird box.
explanation.definitionFit: The sparrow is a small common brown bird found worldwide.
